question.text: A PM holds a Rs. 100 crore FI portfolio with Modified Duration 5. She forecasts a 100 bps rate rise and wants to hedge using 10-year G-Sec futures with lot size Rs. 2 lakh notional and modified duration 8. How many contracts should she SHORT?

explanation.text: The Logic: To hedge interest-rate risk on a fixed-income portfolio with interest-rate futures, the standard duration-based contract-count formula is: Number of contracts = (Portfolio Value × Modified Duration_portfolio) / (Contract Notional × Modified Duration_futures). Applying: (Rs. 100,00,00,000 × 5) / (Rs. 2,00,000 × 8) = 500,00,00,000 / 16,00,000 = 3,125 contracts to be shorted. The Trap: 5,000 ignores the futures' duration; 6,250 uses an incorrect multiplier; 2,500 halves the correct count. None of these properly equate the dollar duration of the hedge to that of the portfolio. Note: The Portfolio Managers (NISM-Series-XXI-B) workbook supports modified duration as a price-sensitivity measure, yield-curve shift risk, and the use of futures as fixed-income hedging tools, but does not explicitly present the (Portfolio × Modified Duration) / (Contract Notional × Futures Modified Duration) formula on the pages checked. The formula and 3,125-contract calculation reflect general industry/regulatory DV01-based hedge construction.
